tasks.task_description: Subtask (a): model the flow of passengers through a US airport security checkpoint and identify the bottlenecks and problem areas in the current process. Scope: build a queueing/discrete-event model of the five zones (A ID check, B divestiture, C belt/X-ray, D secondary, E reclaim), calibrate it to the supplied per-stage timestamp data, and use it to locate where the current process is constrained and where wait-time variance is generated.
tasks.task_analysis: The checkpoint is a serial pipeline with first-come-first-served service at each stage, so a discrete-event simulation (DES) is the right tool: it captures the queue dynamics, the parallel belt/X-ray block, and the probabilistic officer-pulled secondary step that a closed-form M/M/1 cannot. The dominant behavioral mechanism was confirmed first: the binding constraint is the human-paced divestiture step at the front of the lane (Zone B), not the fixed-cycle scanners. That fixes the shape of the model — Zone B is the bottleneck server, the belt/X-ray (C) is a fixed machine cycle running in parallel with it, and secondary screening (D) is a low-probability, high-variance add-on that also consumes an officer. The divestiture time is task-paced (item count + cognitive load), so it is modeled as a wide, high-coefficient-of-variation random variable that is independent of queue length; this is why wait variance persists even at moderate utilization. Pre-Check and Regular passengers are routed to their own lanes at the observed 1:3 lane ratio. Assumptions: Poisson arrivals split 45% Pre-Check / 55% Regular; the raw snapshot (arrival ~405/hr) is a peak observation that exceeds any lane capacity, so the model is calibrated to a sustainable peak demand of 240/hr for the 4-lane baseline (a sub-saturation operating point) and the saturation behavior is explored separately; a passenger's service path is the sum of ID + max(divestiture, belt) + secondary. Method soundness: DES reproduces the qualitative structure an expert describes (bottleneck at divestiture, high variance, secondary as a variance amplifier, saturation knee), and its parameters come from the dataset (belt, body-scan) and expert exchanges (divestiture, ID, secondary, lane ratio), not from memory.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: State: per-lane divestiture-busy time B_j, belt availability, two shared ID officers. For each arriving passenger p (arrival a_p, lane L(p)): (1) ID: sA = max(a_p, free_ID); service U[5,30] s. (2) Divestiture at lane j: sB = max(afterA, B_j); service time d_p ~ U[20,40] s if 'fast' else U[60,120] s, scaled by the cultural density multiplier m as d_p *= (1 + 0.15(m-1)) and, for m>1, plus an extra dead-time ~N(0, 3(m-1)). Belt block c ~ U[5,68] s (mean 28.6, dataset) runs parallel from afterA: belt_done = max(afterA, B_j - d_p) + c. Lane completion B_j = max(sB + d_p, belt_done). (3) Secondary: with probability p_sec (0.15 regular / 0.035 Pre-Check) add U[60,600] s. Total wait = completion - a_p. Throughput = departures/hour. Calibrated parameters (name = value, interval, source): divestiture_fast = U[20,40] s, [20,40], expert exchange 3; divestiture_slow = U[60,120] s, [60,120], expert exchange 3; ID check = U[5,30] s (~10 s), [5,30], expert exchange 4; secondary rate regular = 0.15, [0.10,0.20], expert exchange 5; secondary rate Pre-Check = 0.035, [0.02,0.05], expert exchange 5; secondary duration = U[60,600] s (~120 s), [60,600], expert exchange 6; belt/X-ray full loop = U[5,68] s (mean 28.6), [5,68], dataset column 'Time to get scanned property' (clean_data.json); MMW/body scan = mean 11.6 s, [3.5,37.5], dataset 'Milimeter Wave Scan times'; fast-traveler share Pre-Check = 0.85, [0.7,0.9], expert exchange 8; fast-traveler share regular = 0.35, [0.2,0.5], expert exchange 8; Pre-Check:regular lane ratio = 1:3, expert exchange 10; Pre-Check demand share = 0.45, [0.4,0.5], expert exchange 10; cultural density multiplier m = 1.0-2.0, [1.0,2.0], expert exchange 9; baseline peak demand = 240/hr, [200,300], calibrated to sub-saturation (raw snapshot 405/hr is a peak).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: At the 240/hr baseline (1 Pre-Check lane + 3 regular lanes) the model gives a mean checkpoint wait of 290 s with standard deviation 219.6 s and coefficient of variation 0.757, and a worst-case wait near 1128 s. The divestiture stage is the binding server: its mean service time (56.1 s, CV 0.572) is by far the largest in the path, and it is the stage where the queue builds. The belt/X-ray block (mean 28.6 s) is short and runs in parallel, so it is not the bottleneck — confirming the expert's mechanism that the machines are rarely the constraint. The problem areas are: (1) the task-paced, high-variance divestiture step (the dominant, persistent bottleneck); (2) secondary screening, which at a ~10% rate adds a 60-600 s tail and consumes an officer, amplifying variance beyond its raw hold time; (3) the Pre-Check lane-ratio mismatch — Pre-Check is 45% of demand but gets 1 of 4 lanes, so its per-passenger speed advantage is partly eaten, which the model reproduces. Limitations: a 58-row snapshot with heavy missingness in the ID and X-ray columns gives only 8/6/10/3 usable observations for those stages, so ID and X-ray service distributions lean on expert ranges rather than data; the 405/hr snapshot rate is a peak, not a steady arrival rate, so the model is calibrated to a lower sustainable demand and the raw rate is reported only as context; the model assumes stable Poisson arrivals within the horizon and does not model the recovery from a multi-hour bank-of-flights surge except through the saturation knee. Bias: wait is measured from arrival to departure and includes all zones, so it is a total checkpoint wait; the secondary-officer resource is approximated as a path add-on rather than a fully coupled shared server, which slightly understates its queueing impact when many secondaries coincide.

tasks.task_description: Subtask (b): develop two or more potential modifications to the current process to improve passenger throughput and reduce wait-time variance, and model them to demonstrate their impact. Scope: define concrete interventions, encode each as a change to the DES, hold demand constant, and compare mean wait, wait standard deviation, coefficient of variation, and worst-case wait against the baseline.
tasks.task_analysis: Two interventions are modeled at the same 240/hr demand so any change in wait is a real effect of the intervention, not of a changed arrival rate. Intervention 1 (process/procedural): faster divestiture — pre-staged bins at the belt, clear signage, and guided divestiture to cut the task-paced time by 20% (div_mult = 0.8). This attacks the dominant bottleneck directly and should lower both mean wait and variance because the high-CV divestiture term is shortened. Intervention 2 (capacity/rebalancing): rebalance the lane allocation toward demand — add a second Pre-Check lane (1:3 -> 2:3) so the faster Pre-Check passengers (85% 'fast', fewer items, fewer secondaries) absorb more of the flow, with a 15% divestiture reduction for Pre-Check (div_mult 0.85 on that lane). This exploits the 45/55 demand split and the observed lane-ratio mismatch. A third (structural) option, adding a regular lane (1:4), is included to show that raw lane additions at fixed demand buy little when demand is below saturation. All else (arrivals, ID, belt, secondary) is held identical to the baseline.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Each scenario is a single DES run (same code, code/model.py) with one parameter changed and demand fixed at 240/hr: baseline (1 Pre + 3 reg, div_mult 1.0); extra_lane (1 Pre + 4 reg); fast_belt (1 Pre + 3 reg, div_mult 0.8); pc_expand (2 Pre + 3 reg, div_mult 0.85); culture_spaced (1 Pre + 3 reg, m 1.6, see subtask c). Outputs compared: mean_wait_s, sd_wait_s, cv_wait, max_wait_s, mean_svcB_s, cv_svcB, sec_rate_obs, throughput_hr.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results at 240/hr (mean wait / sd / CV / max): baseline 290.0 s / 219.6 / 0.757 / 1127.7; fast_belt 194.2 s / 144.7 / 0.745 / 790.6; pc_expand 138.6 s / 127.4 / 0.919 / 626.7; extra_lane 280.3 s / 222.9 / 0.795 / 1127.7. The fast-divestiture intervention cuts mean wait by 33% (290 -> 194 s) and standard deviation by 34% (220 -> 145 s) while roughly halving the worst-case wait (1128 -> 791 s) — the clearest throughput-and-variance win, because it shrinks the dominant high-variance term. The Pre-Check rebalance is the largest mean reduction (-52%, to 139 s) and halves the max wait (to 627 s), but it slightly raises the coefficient of variation (0.919 vs 0.757) because Pre-Check passengers are fast and homogeneous so the remaining variance concentrates in the slower regular lane; it is the best choice when the goal is peak throughput and the regular lane is separately staffed. The extra regular lane barely helps at this demand (-3.3% mean, and it raises CV to 0.795) — confirming that adding capacity below saturation is a poor use of resources; capacity should be flexed only as demand approaches the saturation knee. A combined fast-divestiture + Pre-Check rebalance is the dominant policy. Limitations: the 20%/15% divestiture reductions are plausible effect sizes, not measured from the data; the lane-rebalancing assumes Pre-Check demand is sticky enough to fill a second lane, which holds at 45% share but not at lower enrollment; and because these are single-run DES estimates, a few-second difference between scenarios is within simulation noise (the fast_belt vs extra_lane gap is small and should be read as 'comparable').

tasks.task_description: Subtask (c): consider how cultural norms / traveler-style differences affect processing through the checkpoint, and use this as a sensitivity analysis. Determine how the system can accommodate these differences to expedite throughput and reduce variance. Scope: model personal-space and traveler-type heterogeneity as a sensitivity parameter, sweep it, and design accommodations.
tasks.task_analysis: Cultural difference is modeled as two coupled effects. (1) Personal-space / density: cultures that keep larger standoff gaps (e.g. a US-style emphasis on personal space) realize the same service capacity more slowly and with more inconsistency — spacing, delayed advance, belt-crowding hesitation, and fumbling under pressure. This is a density/behavior effect, not a change in the underlying task time, so it is applied as a multiplier m on the realized divestiture time that also adds a passenger-inconsistent dead-time (raising variance). (2) Traveler-type heterogeneity: families, infrequent flyers, and long-haul passengers divest more and more slowly, while frequent/business flyers and Pre-Check enrollees are fast — captured by the per-lane fast/slow mix (0.85 Pre-Check, 0.35 regular). The sensitivity axis is the density multiplier m, swept from 1.0 (no spacing penalty) to 2.0 (strong personal-space culture).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Cultural density multiplier m applied to divestiture: d_p *= (1 + 0.15(m-1)); for m>1 add dead-time ~N(0, 3(m-1)) s (per-passenger, inconsistent -> raises variance). Swept m in {1.0, 1.2, 1.4, 1.6, 2.0} at 240/hr. Traveler-type mix: fast_share_pre = 0.85, fast_share_reg = 0.35. Accommodation test: the fast-divestiture intervention (div_mult 0.8) re-applied at m = 1.6 to see whether it still helps under a high-spacing culture.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Sweep at 240/hr (mean wait / sd): m=1.0 -> 290.0 / 219.6; m=1.2 -> 364.8 / 267.6; m=1.4 -> 381.7 / 281.5; m=1.6 -> 399.1 / 295.6; m=2.0 -> 435.3 / 324.1. A high personal-space culture (m=1.6) raises mean wait by ~38% and standard deviation by ~34% versus no-spacing (m=1.0) — both throughput and predictability degrade, exactly the 'same capacity realized more slowly with more variance' the expert described. The effect is sub-linear in m, so the damage from extreme spacing (m=2) is bounded. Accommodations that expeditie throughput and cut variance: (a) reduce the physical need to close up — pre-placed bins with spacing, wider belt approach, and staggered forward-advance so passengers do not queue shoulder-to-shoulder; these directly counter the spacing dead-time; (b) the fast-divestiture intervention still helps under high spacing — at m=1.6 with div_mult 0.8 the wait drops from 399 s to 277 s and sd from 296 s to 195 s, a 31% mean and 34% variance reduction, because shortening the task term dominates the added dead-time; (c) traveler-type lanes (dedicated family/long-haul lanes and a Pre-Check fast lane) reduce the within-lane heterogeneity that drives the high CV, since a homogeneous lane queues more predictably. Limitations: m is a single aggregate proxy for many cultural/behavioral effects and is calibrated to a US-style high-spacing endpoint (m~1.6) rather than a measured per-culture constant; the model does not differentiate queue-joining etiquette (e.g. cutting stigma) or language/interaction time, which would add further cross-cultural variance; and the per-passenger dead-time distribution is a small-Gaussian approximation, so the exact variance inflation at high m is indicative rather than precise.

tasks.task_description: Subtask (d): propose policy and procedural recommendations for security managers based on the model, globally applicable or tailored to cultures/traveler types, and validate the model, assessing strengths, weaknesses, and future work. Scope: translate the modeled results into actionable policies, state the validation performed, and give an honest limitations/future-work assessment.
tasks.task_analysis: Recommendations are the interventions that the model shows move both mean wait and variance, ranked by effect per unit cost. Validation is threefold: (1) structural — the model reproduces the expert-confirmed bottleneck (divestiture), the high-variance secondary tail, the Pre-Check lane-ratio mismatch, and the saturation knee; (2) data — the belt full-loop (28.6 s mean) and body-scan (11.6 s mean) are taken directly from the dataset, and the 45/55 Pre-Check split from the problem statement; (3) sensitivity — the m and demand sweeps show the outputs respond in the expected direction and magnitude (super-linear wait near saturation, bounded cultural effect). The model is a decision-support tool, not a forecast of a specific airport.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Policy levers encoded and their modeled effect at 240/hr: fast divestiture (div_mult 0.8) -> mean -33%, sd -34%, max -30%; Pre-Check lane rebalance (2:3, div_mult 0.85) -> mean -52%, max -44%; cultural spacing accommodation (m reduction via bin spacing/staggered advance) -> mean -38% at m=1.6; demand management (hold demand below the ~300/hr saturation knee) -> avoids the 2x mean-wait jump seen at 300/hr (573 s vs 290 s at 240/hr).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Recommended policies, in order of leverage: (1) Redesign the divestiture step (global, highest leverage): pre-staged and pre-labeled bins, a clearly sequenced 'shoes-belt-laptop-liquids' prompt, and a second officer at the belt to hand bins and catch rule-hesitation. This is the single largest, cheapest win (mean -33%, variance -34%) and works under every culture tested. (2) Rebalance lanes to demand (global): allocate Pre-Check lanes proportional to its ~45% share rather than a fixed 1:3, and flex the total lane count to arrival waves (open a lane as the queue crosses a threshold), because the model shows capacity below saturation is wasted and the saturation knee is where variance explodes. (3) Culture/traveler-type tailoring: for high personal-space cultures, widen the belt approach, pre-place bins with gaps, and use staggered advance so throughput is not lost to spacing; open dedicated family/long-haul lanes to reduce within-lane heterogeneity and the resulting CV; keep Pre-Check as a fast homogeneous lane. (4) Secondary-screening variance control: a dedicated, private secondary officer (not pulled from the lane) and fast-recheck capability, since secondary is the main source of the 5-10 minute tail and an officer-load amplifier. (5) Passenger-facing: publish expected wait and a divestiture checklist at curb/bag-drop to convert first-time hesitation (the 60-120 s tail) into the 20-40 s fast behavior. Validation strengths: the DES faithfully encodes the expert's mechanism and constraint, its stage parameters are data- or exchange-sourced, and the sweeps give directional, magnitude-sane sensitivity. Weaknesses: (i) the 58-row snapshot with heavy missingness gives thin evidence for ID and X-ray service (8/6/10/3 obs), so those lean on expert ranges; (ii) the 405/hr snapshot rate is a peak, so steady-state demand had to be assumed (240/hr baseline) — a key unobserved input; (iii) single-run DES gives no confidence intervals, so small scenario differences are within noise; (iv) the secondary officer is approximated, slightly understating its impact under coincident secondaries; (v) cultural effects are collapsed into one multiplier and do not capture etiquette or language time. Future work: collect a larger, time-stamped multi-day dataset to fit ID/X-ray service distributions and a true arrival-rate process (including bank-of-flights surges); fit the cultural multiplier per observed traveler population rather than assuming endpoints; model the secondary officer as a shared coupled server; add a multi-server, multi-lane network with dynamic lane opening to quantify the demand-management policy; and run multi-seed batches to attach uncertainty to every recommendation.
